scores.note: Hits all four wanted tropes on a court engine, but the hook needs two clauses to land, the erased-memory midpoint leans on a second magic, and Corvin risks reading as too safe for the comp promise.
Very clear hook with lethal survival pressure. The honesty loophole sits close to the banned miscommunication trope, and the one-couple-per-book structure splits read-through.

It uses a proven pairing (arranged marriage plus secret mission) on a court engine. A lethal love interest disciplines his power, the one-line hook is strong, and each book ends on a hinge with the same couple.

why: A Name Held in Trust delivers the owner's core comp: a competent, underestimated heroine and a dangerous man whose tenderness is selective, paired in a combination that supplies both proximity and opposition. Its hook lands in one sentence: he knows why she came and gives her the name anyway. The trilogy runs on a single costly rule, with a clean hinge in the Emperor holding Elin's own name, and it keeps one couple throughout, which protects Kindle Unlimited read-through.
owner_watch: The bible must rule that the true name is never used, or threatened, to command anything in an intimate or sexual context, and that consent to every intimate beat is freely given and stated on the page. The Book 2 name-split, where the two holders share memories and wounds, must not blur whose consent is whose.
